content.title: Was Jesus simply a great teacher?
content.summary: The eternal Son became truly human to save sinners.

answer.text: Jesus is more than a great teacher: he is the eternal Son of God, truly God and truly man, without sin. He did not cease to be divine when he became human. His person and saving work belong together.

reasoning.text: John identifies the Word as God and as the maker of all created things.
That same Word becomes flesh and dwells among us.
Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as his Lord and God; John calls readers to believe in this Christ.

conclusion.text: Christian faith receives Jesus as Lord and Saviour, not merely as one teacher alongside others.

sections.text: Thomas's confession follows his doubt and Jesus' invitation to examine the wounds. John connects this testimony to life through faith in Christ. Read the scene as the Gospel presents it before considering objections to its truth.
sections.title: Read the encounter, not a slogan

sections.text: Christ shares our humanity, yet without our sin. As our high priest he understands weakness and brings us to God. His deity does not make his suffering pretend, and his humanity does not reduce him to a creature.
sections.title: Why his humanity matters

sections.text: Jesus is not known only from his followers. Within about a century of his death, a Jewish historian and three Roman writers mention him or his movement. Josephus, in the 90s, calls James “the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ”, and in a passage later expanded by Christian copyists describes Jesus as a wise man and wonder-worker condemned by Pilate. Tacitus, about 115, says Christus was executed by Pilate under Tiberius. Pliny the Younger, governor in Asia Minor about 112, reports that Christians met before dawn and, in Melmoth's translation, “addressed a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity”. None of them was friendly, and none supposed Jesus a myth. They establish that he lived, was executed, and was worshipped very early. The texts themselves are read slowly in “Did Jesus exist? What non-Christian writers say”.
sections.title: What writers outside the church said

sections.text: A sceptic may say John's Gospel came late and raised Jesus higher than he raised himself. So start with Mark, by common consent the earliest Gospel. There Jesus tells a paralysed man his sins are forgiven, and the scribes object at once: who can forgive sins but God alone? He calls himself the Son of Man, the figure in Daniel's vision who comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom. At his trial, asked whether he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, he answers “I am” and adds Daniel's words; the high priest tears his clothes and the council condemns him for blasphemy. In material Matthew and Luke share, he says that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son reveals him. The Baptist apologist E. Y. Mullins, setting out this picture in 1905 from the first three Gospels alone, asked whether a man would go to his death for a misunderstood metaphor. And Paul, writing within about twenty-five years, applies to Jesus the words Isaiah used of the one God: every knee will bow. The article “What did Jesus claim about himself?” takes the evidence further.
sections.title: What Jesus claimed in the earliest Gospels

sections.text: If Jesus made claims like these, “a great teacher and nothing more” is the one verdict the evidence does not leave open. The Edinburgh Hebrew scholar John Duncan put it in the 1860s as a trilemma: Christ either deceived mankind by conscious fraud, or was himself deluded, or was divine. C. S. Lewis made the argument famous in his wartime broadcasts. Critics answer with a fourth option, that the claims are legend added later; the answer to that depends on how early the claims are found, which is why Mark and Paul matter. The options are set side by side in “Lord, liar, lunatic, or legend?”.
sections.title: Teacher, deceiver, deluded, or Lord?

sections.text: Christians do not say Jesus was a man who became divine, nor God dressed up as a man. The Council of Chalcedon in 451 confessed one and the same Son, complete in Godhead and complete in manhood, truly God and truly man, like us in all things except sin, known in two natures without confusion, change, division or separation. The Baptist Faith and Message says the same in its own words: Christ is “fully God, fully man”. This is why the Gospels can show him hungry, tired, weeping and not knowing the day of his return, and also forgiving sins, receiving worship and stilling the storm. Both belong to the one person.
sections.title: Truly God and truly man

content.objection: Could we keep Jesus' ethics and leave his divine identity aside?

reply.text: You can examine his teaching, but that would omit the identity and authority the Gospels give him. Jesus calls people to honour the Son as they honour the Father.

heldBy: Bart D. Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014)
Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics
objections.objection: The divine Jesus belongs to John's Gospel, written around the 90s. In Mark, Matthew and Luke he preaches the kingdom of God, not himself; the high claims were put in his mouth by later believers as their devotion grew.

reply.text: The high claims are not confined to John. Mark already has Jesus forgiving sins on his own authority, taking Daniel's Son of Man as his own title, and being condemned for blasphemy. Paul's letters, earlier than any Gospel, worship Jesus with Isaiah's words for the one God and quote what may be an older hymn. Even Ehrman grants that Christians called Jesus divine within a few years of his death; he disputes what they meant by it. Hurtado and Bauckham argue that Jewish monotheists placing a man inside the worship of Israel's God so early has no good explanation by gradual growth.

objections.objection: God cannot be a servant, die, or be exalted by another. Isaac of Troki argued that if Jesus were divine, the prophet could not call him a servant, and Jesus himself said no one is good except God. The Qur'an calls Jesus a messenger and tells Christians not to say “three”.

reply.text: Christians agree that the divine nature does not die or grow. What they confess is that the eternal Son took a full human nature, so that he could serve, obey and die as a man while remaining who he always was. Philippians 2 says exactly this: being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant. When Jesus asks “Why do you call me good?”, he is pressing the young man to think about what he is saying, not denying his own goodness, which the Gospels assert elsewhere. The site's article on the Islamic Jesus takes up the Qur'an's case at length.

heldBy: the liberal Protestant lives of Jesus of the nineteenth century, as Schweitzer describes them
objections.objection: Strip away the miracles and the claims, and what remains, the Sermon on the Mount and the parables, is the real and lasting Jesus. Nineteenth-century writers did exactly this and found a teacher of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man.

reply.text: Schweitzer's history of those lives found that each writer's Jesus looked remarkably like the writer, and concluded that the Jesus of liberal theology never existed. The teaching cannot be cut away from the teacher: the Sermon on the Mount itself ends with Jesus making himself the judge on the last day, and its “but I say to you” sets his word beside the law of God. To admire the ethics and ignore the claims is to choose a Jesus the sources do not give.

limit.text: Recognising what a passage claims and trusting Christ are distinguishable. Salvation is God's gift, received through faith; skill in argument cannot produce new life by itself, because the new birth is the Spirit's work.

prompt.text: Could we read John's account together and ask who Jesus says he is?
